content: Each year, over 200,000 women worldwide are diagnosed with ovarian cancer, and approximately 125,000 die from the disease. This corresponds to an incidence rate of 6.6 cases per 100,000 women and a mortality rate of 4 deaths per 100,000 women, as reported by GLOBOCAN in 2002. Ovarian cancer is the eighth most common cancer globally and the fifth leading cause of cancer-related deaths in women. It accounts for more deaths than any other cancer of the female reproductive system. The majority of ovarian cancer cases are diagnosed at an advanced stage, with 75% to 80% of women presenting with stage III or IV disease at the time of diagnosis. The median time to disease progression (TTPD) ranges from 12 to 20 months, and the median survival time is between 2 and 3 years. However, these outcomes can vary significantly depending on the criteria used to define disease progression and the characteristics of the treated population. The standard initial treatment for advanced ovarian cancer involves a combination of optimal cytoreductive surgery and chemotherapy with a platinum-based agent, most commonly carboplatin and paclitaxel. This approach achieves clinical remission in 70% to 80% of patients. Unfortunately, 62% of these patients will experience a relapse and require additional chemotherapy. The response to second-line chemotherapy is often influenced by the platinum-free interval. Patients who relapse more than six months after completing platinum-based chemotherapy are considered platinum-sensitive and are likely to respond to further platinum-based treatments. High response rates are observed when platinum agents are combined with paclitaxel or gemcitabine. However, treatment options are less well-defined for patients who either do not respond to initial therapy or relapse within six months of completing treatment. These patients are classified as platinum-resistant. Platinum-resistant patients have limited therapeutic options and are typically treated with sequential regimens involving multiple agents. Drugs such as altretamine, bevacizumab, cyclophosphamide, docetaxel, gemcitabine, ifosfamide, irinotecan, liposomal doxorubicin, melphalan, oxaliplatin, topotecan, and vinorelbine have demonstrated activity against ovarian cancer. Common second-line agents include gemcitabine, topotecan, and pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD). However, comparisons of response rates across non-randomized phase II studies have not identified any single agent as superior to the others. Research efforts are now focused on identifying effective treatments for patients with platinum-resistant or recurrent ovarian cancer following platinum-based chemotherapy. Gemcitabine, also known as 2',2'-difluoro 2'-deoxycytidine (dFdC), is a cytidine analogue with unique cellular pharmacology, metabolism, and mechanisms of action. After entering the cell via nucleoside transporters, gemcitabine undergoes intracellular conversion to its active nucleotide forms, gemcitabine diphosphate (dFdCDP) and gemcitabine triphosphate (dFdCTP). These metabolites are responsible for its cytotoxic effects. The cytotoxic activity of gemcitabine is primarily due to its interference with DNA synthesis. dFdCTP competes with deoxycytidine triphosphate (dCTP) to inhibit DNA polymerase. Additionally, dFdCDP inhibits ribonucleoside reductase, leading to a depletion of deoxyribonucleotide pools required for DNA synthesis, thereby enhancing the effects of dFdCTP. dFdCTP is also incorporated into DNA, and the subsequent addition of one more nucleotide results in DNA strand termination. This additional nucleotide may protect dFdCTP from DNA repair enzymes, as its incorporation into DNA appears to resist normal repair mechanisms. Gemcitabine was first identified as a potential therapy for ovarian cancer in 1991 and was recognized as a well-tolerated drug with activity in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer patients by 1994. It has been evaluated in several phase I and II clinical trials as a second-line chemotherapy agent, demonstrating both safety and efficacy. Treatment regimens have varied, with doses ranging from 800 to 1250 mg/m² administered weekly for three weeks, followed by a one-week rest period. The specific regimen depends on prior chemotherapy exposure and observed toxicities. Studies of gemcitabine monotherapy in platinum-resistant or recurrent ovarian cancer have shown overall response rates between 14% and 22%, with a median duration of response ranging from 4.0 to 10.6 months. Myelosuppression associated with gemcitabine is not cumulative and can be managed with dose adjustments. Non-hematological toxicities, such as transient elevations in hepatic transaminases, myalgia, flu-like symptoms, extremity edema, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and headache, are generally mild. However, severe adverse effects, including palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, pulmonary toxicity, and radiation recall, have been reported in some cases. An increasing number of studies are investigating the effects of combining gemcitabine with other agents, such as carboplatin, topotecan, etoposide, paclitaxel, and pertuzumab, in the treatment of platinum-resistant or recurrent ovarian cancer. Hematologic toxicity appears to be more common when gemcitabine is used in combination with other agents, such as paclitaxel or carboplatin. A Cochrane systematic review based on evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is necessary to evaluate the clinical efficacy and adverse effects of gemcitabine in patients with platinum-resistant or recurrent ovarian cancer.
